title: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis Cluster | Neurogenic Claudication
purpose: Clinical prediction rule of Cook (five history/observation items) for lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication.
structure: Spinal canal / intervertebral foramen narrowed by degenerative change (osteophytes, ligamentum flavum thickening, spondylarthrosis, disc protrusion) entrapping cord or root.
procedure: Five items: bilateral neurological symptoms (pain, sensory change, weakness in both legs); leg pain more than back pain; pain on walking or standing (canal and foramen narrow); relief on sitting; age > 48 years (typically > 60).
positive: 0 positive items helps rule out (sensitivity 96%, LR− 0.19); 4 or more positive items helps rule in (specificity 98%, LR+ 4.6).

accuracy.source: Cook et al. (text says 2010; reference list 2011)

notes: Page rates the rule's practical use as moderate. Other stenosis tests: modified Romberg sign, two-stage treadmill test, Kemp's test.

title: Kemp's Test | Extension Quadrant | Lumbar Stenosis
purpose: Provoke neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis and facet joint irritation by recreating foraminal narrowing in extension (also called quadrant test or extension quadrant).
structure: Intervertebral foramina and facet joints of the lumbar spine. Neurogenic claudication: back, buttock and thigh pain, reduced strength and sensation, heaviness/weakness of the legs, provoked by extension in standing and walking.
procedure: Patient standing. Assist maximal spinal extension by holding the shoulders, then have the patient rotate and side-bend toward the painful side.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's symptoms: symptoms matching neurogenic claudication suggest stenosis; predominant pain suggests degenerative facet joint disease.
notes: Other stenosis tests: Cook's clinical prediction rule, modified Romberg sign, two-stage treadmill test.

title: Modified Romberg Sign | Lumbar Stenosis | Neurogenic Claudication
purpose: Balance test with eyes closed for 10 seconds used to help confirm lumbar spinal stenosis.
structure: Proprioceptive/sensory pathways affected by stenosis; the original Romberg test separates sensory from cerebellar ataxia.
procedure: Patient stands with feet together and eyes closed for 10 seconds.
positive: Compensatory movements are needed to keep the feet planted. (Original Romberg: marked loss of stability with eye closure = sensory dysfunction; negative sign with ataxia points to cerebellar disease.)

accuracy.source: Katz et al. 1995, cited via Cook et al. systematic review (text 2019, reference list 2020)

notes: Moderate to confirm, not to exclude stenosis. De Schepper et al. 2013 concluded diagnosis should rest on history and that physical tests were not useful; Cook et al. later found some tests useful for confirmation. Functional tests make sense because claudication is activity-related. Other tests: Cook's CPR, two-stage treadmill, Kemp's.

title: Two-Stage Treadmill Test | Lumbar Stenosis | Neurogenic Claudication
purpose: Compare walking tolerance and symptom onset on a level versus inclined treadmill to help confirm lumbar spinal stenosis (Fritz et al. 1997).
structure: Spinal canal cross-sectional area, which increases when lumbar lordosis decreases on an incline.
procedure: Walk on a level treadmill for 10 minutes; rest 10 minutes; walk on a 15° incline for 10 minutes.
positive: Earlier symptom onset with level walking, prolonged recovery after level walking, or longer total walking time on the incline.

accuracy.source: Fritz et al. 1997, cited via Cook et al. systematic review (text 2019, reference list 2020); imaging was the reference standard although stenosis is a clinical diagnosis

notes: Good to confirm, not to exclude stenosis. See modified Romberg record for the De Schepper 2013 versus Cook context. Other tests: Cook's CPR, modified Romberg, Kemp's.

title: Prone Instability Test | Radiographic Lumbar Instability Assessment
purpose: Assess radiographic lumbar instability as a possible cause of chronic low back pain, and whether the patient can actively stabilize the spine (relevant to stabilization exercise).
structure: Lumbar segments under posterior-anterior pressure, with and without active extensor muscle stabilization.
procedure: Part 1: patient prone with the legs over the end of the bench, feet on the floor; apply PA pressure to each lumbar segment to provoke pain. Part 2: if painful, the patient lifts the feet off the floor and PA pressure is repeated.
positive: Pain provoked in part 1 is reduced in part 2 (patient can actively stabilize), which also suggests suitability for a stabilization exercise programme.

accuracy.source: Fritz et al. 2005; Ferrari et al. 2015 review; inter-rater kappa 0.46-0.87 (Hicks 2003, Schneider 2008, Rabin 2013)

notes: Poor diagnostic test for radiographic instability per the page, but a component of the Hicks stabilization CPR. SOURCE NOTE: this page embeds the same YouTube ID as the passive lumbar extension test page. Related: passive lumbar extension, interspinous gap change, low midline sill sign.

title: Passive Lumbar Extension Test | Radiographic Lumbar Instability Assessment
purpose: Physical test (PLET) indicating lumbar spine instability.
procedure: Patient prone. Both legs are passively raised about 30 cm from the bench and gently pulled.
positive: Severe low back pain, a feeling of heaviness in the lower back, or a feeling that the lower back is about to 'come off'.

accuracy.source: Kasai et al. 2006; Ferrari et al. 2014; inter-rater kappa 0.76 (Rabin et al. 2013)

notes: Page rates it moderately useful; the best diagnostic value for instability is a cluster of subjective and objective findings. SOURCE NOTE: same YouTube ID as the prone instability test page. Related: prone instability, interspinous gap change, low midline sill sign.

title: Low Midline Sill Sign | Radiographic Lumbar Instability & Spondylolisthesis
purpose: Inspection/palpation sign (also slipping palpation or step-off sign) for lumbar spondylolisthesis and radiographic instability.
structure: Spinous processes; the superior process displaced anteriorly relative to the inferior one forms a sill shaped like a capital L.
procedure: Patient stands with the back exposed. Observe the midline for a sill, then run a thumb down the spinous processes.
positive: The superior spinous process is felt displaced anterior to the inferior one, usually tender.

accuracy.source: Petersen et al. 2017 review (slipping palpation); original description Ahn & Jhun 2015

notes: At least moderately useful despite wide confidence intervals and real-life limits such as obesity. SOURCE NOTE: the page's header section is titled 'Interspinous Gap Change' (copy error). Related: prone instability, passive lumbar extension, interspinous gap change.
status: ok (header title copy error on source)

title: Interspinous Gap Change | Radiographic Lumbar Instability & Spondylolisthesis
purpose: Palpation test during flexion-extension for lumbar spondylolisthesis and radiographic instability.
structure: Interspinous spaces and spinous process alignment during flexion and extension.
procedure: Patient stands about one leg length from the table, feet shoulder-width apart, flexes forward with both hands on the table edge. Inspect and palpate the spine cranial to caudal for a level that looks bent or has a wider gap; place a thumb on each adjacent spinous process and ask the patient to extend by pushing the pelvis toward the table while palpating.
positive: The interspinous space abruptly narrows compared with other levels, or the upper spinous process shifts anteriorly or posteriorly relative to the lower one; tenderness is usual at wide-gap levels.

accuracy.source: Ahn & Jhun 2015 (vs flexion-extension radiographs, cut-offs 10° sagittal rotation / 4 mm translation)

notes: First and only study, and no consensus on defining instability, so clinical value at most moderate. Related: prone instability, passive lumbar extension, low midline sill sign.

title: Lumbar Motor Control Impairment (MCI) | Signs & Symptoms
purpose: Expert-consensus (Delphi, Cook et al. 2006) signs and symptoms of clinical lumbar instability / motor control impairment, since no validated test or gold standard exists.
structure: Lumbar segments with an enlarged neutral zone (Panjabi concept); local stabilizing muscles.
procedure: Top five subjective items: feeling of giving way; frequent self-manipulation (cracking the back); frequent episodes; painful catching or locking on twisting/bending; pain during transitional activities (e.g. sit to stand). Top five objective items: poor lumbopelvic control with segmental hinging/pivoting and poor proprioception; poor coordination/neuromuscular control (juddering, shaking); decreased strength and endurance of local muscles at the unstable level; aberrant movements including a changing lateral shift during AROM; pain with sustained positions.
positive: A patient showing many of these items would logically be expected to benefit from a stabilization programme.
notes: Avoid nocebo: do not tell patients their back is unstable; frame it as finding out whether an exercise programme is an option. Related: motor control dysfunction screening (Luomajoki), local stabilizers assessment, and the radiographic instability tests.

title: Motor Control Dysfunction Screening | Test Battery by Luomajoki
purpose: Six-test battery (Luomajoki et al. 2007) to assess movement control dysfunction in non-specific, mechanical low back pain.
structure: Lumbopelvic movement control. Context on the page: only 10% of low back pain is specific; of the 90% non-specific, about a third is non-mechanical (central/psychosocial) and 70% mechanical, movement- or posture-dependent.
procedure: 1) Waiter's bow: hip hinge with neutral spine. 2) Posterior pelvic tilt (lumbar flexion). 3) Single-leg stance: feet one third of the inter-trochanteric distance apart, stand on one leg, measure lateral shift (norm 8 cm; > 2 cm side difference abnormal). 4) Sitting knee extension with corrected lordosis and no lumbar flexion. 5) Forward and backward rocking in four-point kneeling without extending/flexing the low back. 6) Prone knee bend: heel to buttock without moving the back. Standardized instructions; re-explain and demonstrate once if misunderstood.
positive: Inability to perform a test correctly (loss of conscious lumbar movement control) as illustrated by the correct/incorrect images.

accuracy.source: n/a; Luomajoki et al. 2007: intra- and inter-rater kappa > 0.6, no difference between novice and experienced raters, clear difference between patients and healthy subjects

notes: Correct/incorrect example images are not in the API text. Also cites O'Sullivan 2000. Related: MCI signs & symptoms, local stabilizers assessment.

title: Lumbar Local Stabilizers Assessment | Pressure Biofeedback Unit
purpose: Assess and retrain recruitment of the local lumbar stabilizers (transversus abdominis, multifidi) with the abdominal draw-in manoeuvre (ADIM) and a pressure biofeedback unit.
procedure: Step 1, four-point kneeling: neutral spine, relax the abdomen on a deep exhalation, pull the navel toward the spine and hold up to 10 s without breathing; 10 × 10 s, progressing to 3 × 90 s. Step 2, prone: cuff under the abdomen inflated to 70 mmHg; after one breath, hold the breath and perform ADIM, aiming for a 2-4 mmHg pressure drop, 10 × 10 s; watch for oblique compensation (excessive pressure drop). Step 3, supine: cuff under L3 at 40 mmHg; ADIM should raise pressure in 2-4 mmHg steps while breathing calmly, held 15 s twice.
positive: Target pressure changes as above without compensation.

accuracy.lr_plus: close to 1 (pressure biofeedback vs ultrasound TrA activity)

notes: Physiotutors' critically appraised topic: pressure biofeedback measurements do not correlate with ultrasound-measured transversus abdominis activity and are not a valid tool for detecting TrA dysfunction (likelihood ratios near 1). Related: MCI signs & symptoms, Luomajoki screening.

title: Cluster of van der Wurff | Sacroiliac Joint Pain | SIJ Assessment
purpose: Battery of five SIJ provocation tests to determine whether pain originates from the sacroiliac joint.
structure: Sacroiliac joint; pain must be felt ipsilaterally in the gluteal region below L5.
procedure: Each held about 5 s: distraction (supine, cross-armed pressure on both ASIS dorsolaterally, up to 25-30 kg); compression (side-lying affected side up, hips 45°, knees 90°, downward pressure on the iliac crest, 25-30 kg); thigh thrust (supine, hip 90° slightly adducted, force along the femur, 25-30 kg); Gaenslen (supine at the table edge, contralateral hip fixed in maximal flexion/slight abduction, ipsilateral leg lowered into extension with about 15 kg pressure, affected side only); Patrick's/FABER (contralateral ASIS fixed, ipsilateral knee lowered, 15 kg overpressure).
positive: 3 or more of 5 tests positive. A test counts as positive only if the familiar pain is provoked AND felt ipsilaterally in the gluteal region below L5.
notes: Individual test pages (distraction, compression, thigh thrust, Gaenslen, Patrick's) and the Cluster of Laslett are in the hip module.

title: Active Straight Leg Raise Test | Pelvic Girdle Pain
purpose: Test the ability to transfer load between the lower limb and trunk in pelvic girdle pain (posterior pelvic pain since pregnancy).
structure: Lumbopelvic load transfer / force closure of the sacroiliac joint.
procedure: Patient supine, legs straight and relaxed in lateral rotation, feet 20 cm apart; raise each leg in turn 5 cm off the couch without bending the knee. If painful or difficult, repeat with manual compression of both ASIS or with a sacroiliac belt. Scoring 0-5 per side (0 no difficulty, 5 unable); a summed score of 0 is negative, 1-10 positive.
positive: Difficulty/pain lifting the leg that is abolished by pelvic compression (reduced force closure). In excessive force closure the test is usually negative and compression may provoke (O'Sullivan et al. 2007).

accuracy.source: Mens et al. 2001 (healthy vs posterior pelvic pain since pregnancy; test-retest reliability 0.87 at 1 week)

notes: Page rates high clinical value. Scores correlate with pelvic joint mobility (Mens 1999) and with Quebec Back Pain Disability Scale (Mens 2002, usable as severity scale). Mens & Pool-Goudzwaard 2017: transversus abdominis is excessively active during ASLR in long-lasting pregnancy-related PGP, so there is no rationale for TrA-activation exercises. SOURCE NOTE: the page's header section is titled 'Yeoman Test | Sacroiliitis Examination' (copy error).
status: ok (header title copy error on source)

title: Standing Bent Over Test | Vorlauf Test | SIJ Dysfunction Assessment
purpose: Palpation test (also Vorlauf or standing flexion test) for sacroiliac joint 'dysfunction' (hypomobility).
structure: PSIS movement relative to the sacrum during forward bending; counternutation normally starts around 60° flexion.
procedure: Patient standing; palpate both PSIS and ask the patient to bend forward; judge whether both PSIS move symmetrically.
positive: The PSIS on one side moves further cranially (earlier) = hypomobile side.
notes: Weak value; Physiotutors advise abandoning SIJ dysfunction tests in favour of provocation tests such as the Cluster of Laslett (hip module). SOURCE NOTE: the page embeds the same YouTube ID as the Gillet test page (hip module). Related: Shimpi prone SIJ test, Gillet, SIJ nutation/counternutation.
status: ok (shares video ID with gillet-test in hip module)

title: Shimpi Prone SI Joint Test | SIJ Dysfunction Assessment
purpose: Newer test for sacroiliac joint dysfunction proposed by Shimpi et al. 2018.
structure: Sacroiliac joint / ASIS movement during prone hip extension.
procedure: Patient prone. Examiner on the symptomatic side places a palm under the ASIS; the patient extends the hip to about 15° so the leg lifts slightly off the table.
positive: The ASIS lifts off the examiner's palm with reproduction of familiar SIJ pain. Negative: the ASIS presses into the hand and no pain.

accuracy.source: Shimpi et al. 2018 (45 participants, first study, no fluoroscopically guided block as reference standard)

notes: Weak clinical value per the page; SIJ dysfunction tests are unreliable and should probably be abandoned in favour of provocation tests. Related: standing bent-over, Gillet, SIJ nutation/counternutation (hip module).

title: Lumbar Stabilization CPR | Clinical Prediction Rule by Hicks
purpose: Clinical prediction rule (Hicks et al. 2005) to identify low back pain patients likely to benefit from a stabilization exercise programme.
structure: Subgrouping of heterogeneous chronic low back pain; programme targeted transversus abdominis, multifidus, quadratus lumborum and obliques.
procedure: Success rule, 3 or more of 4: age < 40 years; straight leg raise > 90°; aberrant motions during lumbar AROM; positive prone instability test. Failure rule, 2 or more of 4: FABQ activity subscale ≤ 8; no aberrant movement; negative prone instability test; no hypomobility on the lumbar spring test.
positive: ≥3/4 success items: odds of success with stabilization × 4.0. ≥2/4 failure items: odds of success × 0.18.

accuracy.source: Hicks et al. 2005 (values are likelihood ratios for treatment success, not diagnostic accuracy)

notes: Page remarks that less fearful patients (FABQ-A ≤ 8) had worse odds with a stabilization programme. Companion: Flynn manipulation CPR.

title: Lumbar Manipulation CPR | Clinical Prediction Rule by Flynn
purpose: Clinical prediction rule (Flynn et al. 2002, validated by Childs et al. 2004) to identify low back pain patients likely to improve with lumbar manipulation.
structure: Subgrouping of low back pain; hip-spine relationship (hip internal rotation).
procedure: Five criteria: no symptoms distal to the knee; symptom duration < 16 days; FABQ work subscale < 19; lumbar hypomobility; hip internal rotation > 35° in at least one hip.
positive: ≥3 of 5: likelihood of success × 2.61; ≥4 of 5: × 24.38; all 5: described as increasing 'indefinitely'. ≤2 items: consider another approach, e.g. stabilization.

accuracy.source: Flynn et al. 2002; Childs et al. 2004 validation (manipulation + exercise beat exercise alone in this subgroup); values are likelihood ratios for treatment success

notes: Rationale on the page: distal symptoms suggest radicular syndrome (conflicting evidence for manipulation, excluded by Flynn); chronic cases carry psychosocial factors; low hip IR suggests mobilizing the hip instead (hip-spine dilemma). Companion: Hicks stabilization CPR.

title: Direction-specific Exercises for Low Back Pain
purpose: Use directional preference and centralization (McKenzie 'derangement' concepts) to choose repeated movements that modify symptoms in acute low back pain with or without radiculopathy.
structure: Lumbar spine; directional preference = repeated flexion, extension or lateral flexion progressively abolishes symptoms or increases range; centralization = spinal and referred pain abolished distal to proximal with repeated movements.
procedure: Identify the preferred direction and have the patient perform repeated movements in it; the video shows Physiotutors' practical examples (explicitly not a strict McKenzie application).
notes: May & Aina 2012 review: 70% of patients show a directional preference; 44% centralize (74% in acute LBP, 42% if persistent or over 65); centralization was a treatment effect modifier in 7 of 8 studies. Also cites Laslett 2009 (manual correction of lateral shift). The second YouTube link on the page (Jarod Hall) is a reference, not an embed, so only one video is listed.
